transcript: In 1960, a 26-year-old English woman named Jane Goodall Walked alone into the forest of Tanzania in East Africa Her aim was to observe wild chimpanzees In their own natural environment In those days it was almost unprecedented For a woman to enter the interior of Africa by herself She did not even have a university degree But the paleontologist Louis Leakey believed in her passion and patience and supported her. In the forest of Gombe, she sat for months without showing herself deep among the trees. After a while the chimpanzees stopped fearing her And began to show her glimpses of their daily lives Her greatest discovery was the observation That chimpanzees made twigs into tools for catching termites To the world of science which had until then believed That only humans used tools This came as a great shock Goodall also showed that chimpanzees had emotions similar To those of humans' family bonds, sadness and conflict Her observations redrew from the very ground The line between humanity and other animals In her later years, Goodall devoted herself To the conservation of wildlife The youth program she founded, called Roots and Shoots Has become a starting point for young people in over 60 countries to take on environmental issues in their own neighborhoods. segments.text: In 1960, a 26-year-old English woman named Jane Goodall
Walked alone into the forest of Tanzania in East Africa
Her aim was to observe wild chimpanzees
In their own natural environment
In those days it was almost unprecedented
For a woman to enter the interior of Africa by herself
She did not even have a university degree
But the paleontologist Louis Leakey believed in her passion and patience and supported her.
In the forest of Gombe, she sat for months without showing herself deep among the trees.
After a while the chimpanzees stopped fearing her
And began to show her glimpses of their daily lives
Her greatest discovery was the observation
That chimpanzees made twigs into tools for catching termites
To the world of science which had until then believed
That only humans used tools
This came as a great shock
Goodall also showed that chimpanzees had emotions similar
To those of humans' family bonds, sadness and conflict
Her observations redrew from the very ground
The line between humanity and other animals
In her later years, Goodall devoted herself
To the conservation of wildlife
The youth program she founded, called Roots and Shoots
Has become a starting point for young people in over 60 countries
to take on environmental issues in their own neighborhoods.
Hope lies in action.
Her words remain even now.
A steady encouragement for the many young people
who carry concern for the future.
